title: HE STOOD BESIDE DAVID WHEN DEATH WAS NEAR—SO WHY DID SOLOMON STRIP HIM OF THE PRIESTHOOD?
paragraphs: HE STOOD BESIDE DAVID WHEN DEATH WAS NEAR—SO WHY DID SOLOMON STRIP HIM OF THE PRIESTHOOD?
The heartbreaking downfall of Abiathar reveals a terrifying truth about misplaced loyalty, the consequences of compromise, and the mercy of God that can still reach us after everything falls apart.
Imagine surviving the massacre of your entire family.
Imagine watching the people you love die because a powerful king believes they have helped his enemy.

You escape with your life. You carry the weight of everything you have lost. And somehow, in the middle of that unimaginable grief, you find yourself serving alongside a man who will one day become Israel's greatest king.
You stand with him when he has no throne.
You suffer with him when he has no palace.
You remain with him when being his friend could cost you your life.
Years pass. Battles are fought. Prayers are offered. A kingdom is established.
And then, near the end of your life, the son of that very king looks you in the eyes and tells you that you are no longer worthy to serve as priest.
Not because you abandoned the God of Israel.
Not because you had spent your life worshiping idols.
But because, at a moment when loyalty mattered more than ever, you supported the wrong man.
This is the story of Abiathar.
And before you dismiss it as an ancient political conflict involving kings and priests, understand something.
You can have a remarkable history of faithfulness and still make a devastating decision in the present.
That is what makes this account so unsettling.
Because somewhere between Abiathar's suffering, his years of service, his compromise, and his removal from the priesthood, we may recognize something painfully familiar about ourselves.
The question is not simply why Solomon removed Abiathar.
The deeper question is what happens when someone who has walked with God for years begins trusting something other than God's revealed will.
And the answer takes us from a blood-soaked priestly city to a royal judgment, from an ancient prophecy to the cross of Jesus Christ.
Stay with this story.
Because the most surprising thing about Abiathar's downfall may not be the judgment he received.
It may be the mercy he was shown.
Abiathar's story began with a tragedy almost too terrible to imagine.
In 1 Samuel 21–22, David was fleeing from King Saul. Hungry and desperate, he came to Nob, where Ahimelech the priest gave him bread and the sword of Goliath.
Ahimelech did not realize the full danger surrounding David's visit.
But Doeg the Edomite reported what had happened to Saul.
Saul interpreted the assistance as treason.
What followed was horrifying.
Eighty-five priests wearing the linen ephod were killed, and the city of Nob was struck with the sword, including its inhabitants and livestock (1 Samuel 22:18–19).
One man escaped.
Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech.
He fled to David and told him what had happened.
And David said something that must have pierced both their hearts:
"I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house." — 1 Samuel 22:22, KJV
Then David told Abiathar to remain with him, promising that he would be safe under David's protection (1 Samuel 22:23).
Think about that moment.
A grieving priest who had lost his family.
A fugitive who knew his actions had contributed to the danger.
Two men bound together by suffering, danger, and the uncertain future of a kingdom not yet established.
Abiathar did not join David when David was sitting comfortably on a throne.
He joined him when association with David could be a death sentence.
That matters.
Because Abiathar was not some shallow opportunist who had never sacrificed anything.
He had endured real suffering.
He had remained with David through extraordinary danger.
He had served in a sacred office during one of Israel's most turbulent generations.
And this is precisely why his later decision is so tragic.
Sometimes the people who fall are not people who never stood for anything. Sometimes they are people who stood faithfully for years but stopped watching where their hearts were going.
Perhaps you know something about that.
There was a season when your prayers were desperate and sincere.
You opened your Bible because you genuinely needed to hear from God.
You walked away from relationships, habits, or opportunities because you believed obedience mattered more than comfort.
You remember what God brought you through.
But somewhere along the way, something changed.
Maybe your confidence quietly shifted from God's Word to your own experience.
Maybe you began believing that because you had suffered for the Lord in the past, your present decisions did not require the same humility.
Maybe you became so accustomed to being near holy things that you stopped examining the condition of your heart.
Abiathar's story confronts that danger.
Not because every mistake is identical to his.
But because yesterday's faithfulness cannot replace today's obedience.
And then came the succession crisis.
David was old.
His reign was nearing its end.
And the question of who would sit on Israel's throne had become urgent.
Adonijah, another son of David, declared himself king.
First Kings 1:5 records his ambition:
"I will be king." — 1 Kings 1:5, KJV
Those four words expose something deeply human.
Not, "What has God commanded?"
Not, "Whom has the Lord appointed?"
But, "I will."
Adonijah gathered powerful supporters, including Joab, David's military commander.
And among those who supported him was Abiathar the priest.
First Kings 1:7 says that Adonijah consulted with Joab and Abiathar, and they followed and helped him.
Yet the same chapter identifies Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and others who did not support Adonijah.
This was no harmless disagreement about administrative arrangements.
The throne was at stake.
David had sworn that Solomon would succeed him (1 Kings 1:13, 17, 30). First Chronicles 22:9–10 also presents Solomon as the son designated by God to succeed David and build the temple.
Adonijah's attempt to seize royal authority therefore stood against the succession David had committed himself to establish.
Abiathar had once risked his life by standing beside God's chosen king.
Now he was supporting a rival to the son appointed to succeed that king.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us what motivated Abiathar.
Perhaps he thought Adonijah had the stronger claim because of his age.
Perhaps longstanding relationships influenced him.
Perhaps he misjudged the political situation.
We should not pretend to know what the Bible does not reveal.
But we do know his decision.
He supported Adonijah.
And that decision carried consequences.
Here is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
You do not have to hate God to make a decision that conflicts with His will.
You do not have to publicly renounce your faith to become spiritually careless.
Sometimes compromise begins with a calculation that seems reasonable.
A relationship you do not want to lose.
An opportunity you cannot imagine passing up.
A position you have spent years trying to secure.
A fear that obedience will cost too much.
And suddenly the question becomes less about what God has said and more about what you stand to gain or lose.
Not every difficult choice is a rebellion against God. Scripture calls us to discern carefully rather than invent divine commands where none have been given.
But when God's Word is clear, personal advantage is never a sufficient reason to disobey.
The most dangerous compromise is often the one we have learned to explain to ourselves.
Then David acted.
Bathsheba and Nathan brought the succession crisis before him, and David ordered Solomon to be anointed king.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet participated in Solomon's public anointing (1 Kings 1:32–40).
The people rejoiced.
The city erupted with celebration.
Adonijah's attempt collapsed.
His supporters scattered.
And Abiathar, who had survived Saul's slaughter and served through David's reign, now faced the consequences of having supported a rival claimant.
When David died and Solomon began securing his kingdom, the reckoning came.
First Kings 2:26 records Solomon's words to Abiathar:

"Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou art worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted." — 1 Kings 2:26, KJV
Read that carefully.
Solomon did not pretend Abiathar's betrayal was insignificant.
He regarded Abiathar as deserving death for his involvement in the rebellion.
But he did not execute him.
Why?
Because Solomon remembered.
He remembered that Abiathar had carried the ark before David.
He remembered that Abiathar had shared David's afflictions.
He remembered the years of costly service.
The king who had the power to execute him instead sent him away to his fields in Anathoth.
That is not the same as forgiveness through the Gospel. The passage describes Solomon's royal decision, not Abiathar's personal repentance or eternal standing before God.
But it does reveal a remarkable restraint.
Abiathar's wrongdoing was not ignored.
Yet his past suffering and service were not forgotten.
He lost his priestly position.
But his life was spared.
And sometimes that distinction is easy to overlook when reading the Bible too quickly.
Mercy does not always mean escaping every consequence. Sometimes mercy means receiving less judgment than you deserved.
Perhaps you are living with consequences right now.
A relationship was damaged by words you cannot take back.
Trust was broken by a decision you wish you had never made.
An opportunity disappeared because you ignored warnings.
You have prayed for forgiveness, but the circumstances have not returned to what they were before.
And a painful question keeps rising inside you.
"If God has forgiven me, why am I still dealing with this?"
Abiathar's story does not answer every personal situation. But it reminds us that mercy and consequences can exist together.
David himself experienced that reality after his sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 12:13–14).
Forgiveness does not make sin harmless.
Grace does not mean that every earthly result of our actions disappears.
But consequences do not place a repentant sinner beyond the reach of God's mercy.
That truth becomes even more beautiful when we understand what happened next.
First Kings 2:27 says:
"So Solomon thrust out Abiathar from being priest unto the LORD; that he might fulfil the word of the LORD, which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh." — 1 Kings 2:27, KJV
This is the verse that transforms the entire story.
Abiathar's removal was not merely the result of a political dispute.
The biblical narrator connects it to a prophecy spoken generations earlier.
Long before Solomon became king, long before Abiathar fled the massacre at Nob, a warning had been delivered against the priestly house of Eli.
Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, had treated their sacred responsibilities with contempt.
First Samuel 2 describes their wickedness, including their abuse of priestly privilege and their dishonoring of the Lord's offerings.
Eli confronted his sons, but he failed to restrain their evil adequately.
A man of God then announced judgment upon Eli's house.
The Lord declared:
"Them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed." — 1 Samuel 2:30, KJV
The prophecy continued with the warning that Eli's family would lose its privileged priestly standing and that God would raise up a faithful priest (1 Samuel 2:31–36).
The warning was repeated to Samuel in 1 Samuel 3:11–14.
Now, generations later, the biblical writer points back to that word.
Abiathar belonged to the priestly line associated with Eli, and his removal from office marked the fulfillment of the judgment upon that house.
Consider the weight of that.
A prophecy spoken in Shiloh.
A massacre at Nob.
A surviving priest who fled to David.
Years of faithful service.
A succession crisis.
A final removal from office.
Events separated by generations were brought together in the unfolding history of Israel.
The Hebrew wording of 1 Kings 2:27 makes the connection especially striking.
The expression translated "to fulfil the word of the LORD" includes:
לְמַלֵּא אֶת־דְּבַר יְהוָה
Lemallēʾ ʾet-devar YHWH
Literally, the expression conveys the fulfillment or bringing to completion of the word of the LORD.
The Hebrew verb comes from the root מלא (mlʾ), associated with filling or completing.
The point is not that Solomon suddenly invented a divine reason for a political decision.
The narrator explicitly presents Abiathar's removal as the fulfillment of the previously spoken divine judgment.
And that should humble us.
Because God's Word is not made irrelevant by the passage of time.
Human circumstances change.
Kingdoms rise and fall.
Generations come and go.
But God does not forget what He has spoken.
Isaiah 40:8 declares:
"The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."
There is something both terrifying and comforting about that truth.
Terrifying, because God's warnings are not empty.
Comforting, because His promises are not empty either.
The God who remembered His word concerning Eli is also the God who remembers His covenant promises.
And that brings us to something even deeper.
Why did Solomon remove Abiathar from the priesthood?
The immediate reason was Abiathar's support for Adonijah's attempted seizure of the throne.
The larger biblical explanation was the fulfillment of God's judgment upon Eli's priestly house.
Both truths belong together.
But neither should be distorted.
The passage does not teach that every hardship in your life is punishment for a hidden sin.
It does not give us permission to tell suffering people that their family history has placed them under an unavoidable spiritual curse.
And it does not mean that believers today must fear being condemned for the sins of their ancestors.
Ezekiel 18:20 teaches individual moral responsibility, and the New Testament proclaims freedom from condemnation for those who belong to Christ (Romans 8:1).
Abiathar's account concerns a particular priestly family, a particular office, and a particular judgment in Israel's covenant history.
We honor Scripture by allowing it to say what it says.
Not less.
And not more.
Yet the moral warning remains.
Sacred position is not a substitute for obedience.
Religious experience is not immunity from accountability.
And a long history of ministry does not place anyone above the authority of God's Word.
That warning is especially important for those of us who serve in Christian communities.
You can teach Scripture and still need correction.
You can lead worship and still struggle with pride.
You can preach repentance and still have sins you are reluctant to confess.
You can spend years encouraging others and quietly neglect your own soul.
Even the apostle Paul understood the importance of continued spiritual discipline.
In 1 Corinthians 9:27, he spoke of disciplining his body so that, after preaching to others, he would not himself be disqualified.
This was not an invitation to live in constant terror.
It was a call to take faithfulness seriously.
And perhaps the question we need to ask is not whether we have ever served God faithfully.
Perhaps it is whether we are listening to Him today.
Because a testimony about what God did ten years ago is precious.
But it cannot replace surrender this morning.
There is another remarkable detail in the story.
Solomon removed Abiathar, and Zadok became priest in his place (1 Kings 2:35).
First Chronicles 6:4–8 traces Zadok's ancestry through Eleazar, the son of Aaron.
This priestly transition is part of the historical setting in which the judgment upon Eli's house reached its fulfillment.
Yet we must be careful not to stop at Zadok as though he were the ultimate answer to humanity's need for a faithful priest.
The Old Testament priesthood, even at its best, was never the final solution to human sin.
Priests were themselves sinners.
They grew old.
They died.
Their service continued from one generation to another because none of them could provide the final, once-for-all sacrifice that humanity needed.
And this is where Abiathar's story leads us toward something greater than Israel's political history.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
The New Testament book of Hebrews reveals a High Priest unlike any priest who served under the old covenant.
Jesus did not receive His priesthood through descent from Aaron.
Hebrews 7 explains His priesthood in connection with Melchizedek and the power of an indestructible life.
Hebrews 7:24–25 declares:

"But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them." — KJV
The Greek expression translated "to the uttermost" is:
εἰς τὸ παντελές
Eis to panteles.
It carries the sense of completely, fully, or to the fullest extent.
In this context, Hebrews emphasizes Christ's complete saving ability because He lives forever to intercede for those who come to God through Him.
Think about what that means.
Abiathar's priestly ministry could end.
Zadok's earthly life would eventually end.
Every human priest was limited by mortality.
But Jesus Christ lives forever.
His priesthood does not expire.
His intercession does not cease.
His sacrifice does not need to be repeated.
And His saving power does not weaken with time.
The priesthood of Abiathar could be taken away. The priesthood of Jesus Christ can never be taken away.
That is not merely an interesting theological comparison.
It is the heart of our hope.
Because if your salvation ultimately depended on the unbroken faithfulness of a human priest, you would have reason to tremble.
And if your salvation depended on your own perfect record, you would have no hope at all.
But the Gospel announces that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, offered Himself once for sins and rose victorious over death.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
"For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes genuine repentance possible without despair.
It does not excuse rebellion.
It announces that sinners who turn to Christ can receive forgiveness through His finished work.
And suddenly Abiathar's story forces us to confront a question much closer to home.
What are you trusting to make you right with God?
Your years in church?
Your ministry title?
Your family's Christian background?
The sacrifices you made when you were younger?
The prayers you prayed in a previous season?
Those things may be part of your testimony.
But they cannot save you.
Only Jesus can.
And if you have spent years appearing spiritually strong while quietly drifting from Him, the invitation of the Gospel is not to manufacture another religious performance.
It is to come into the light.
To stop defending what God is calling you to confess.
To stop pretending that a respectable reputation is the same as a surrendered heart.
To turn away from sin and return to Christ.
First John 1:9 gives believers this assurance:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice the beauty of those words.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
God does not ask you to pretend your sin never happened.
He calls you to confess it.
He does not offer forgiveness by declaring evil harmless.
He offers forgiveness through the righteous work of Jesus Christ.
And He does not merely invite you to feel better about your past.
He calls you into a transformed life.
Perhaps that is what makes this story so personal.
Some of us are afraid of being exposed.
Others are afraid of being forgotten.
We fear that one failure will erase every good thing we have ever done.
Or that one terrible decision means there is no future left for us.
But the Gospel speaks a better word than either denial or despair.
Your sin is serious.
Christ's mercy is greater.
Your choices matter.
God's grace is not exhausted.
Your past cannot save you.
Your past does not have to be your final identity either.
And there is one final detail in Abiathar's story that deserves our attention.
After Solomon sent him to Anathoth, Scripture does not give us a detailed account of Abiathar's remaining years.
We are not told whether he repented.
We are not told what conversations he had with his family.
We are not told whether he spent his later days in bitterness, regret, humility, or renewed devotion.
The Bible leaves those questions unanswered.
And we should leave them unanswered too.
But perhaps that silence is what makes the account so haunting.
A man who had stood near the center of Israel's sacred and royal history was sent away from the priesthood.
His public ministry was over.
His former position was gone.
The text records his removal, then moves forward.
No long farewell.
No recorded speech defending his decisions.
No dramatic account of his final days.
Just the sobering reality that his life had reached a turning point from which he would not return to his former office.
And it makes me wonder how many people are living today as though they will always have another opportunity to obey.
Another opportunity to apologize.
Another opportunity to confess.
Another opportunity to reconcile.
Another opportunity to put Christ first.
Another opportunity to become serious about the faith they have been professing for years.
We are not promised endless tomorrows.
Second Corinthians 6:2 reminds us:
"Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation."
Not because God is reluctant to show mercy.
But because postponing repentance is itself a dangerous way to live.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing something in your heart through Scripture, do not bury it beneath another distraction.
If you have been compromising, acknowledge it.
If you have been trusting in religious activity rather than Christ, return to the Gospel.
If you have wounded someone, take responsibility where you can.
If you have wandered from prayer and Scripture, begin again.
And if you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord, do not confuse familiarity with Christianity for saving faith.
Come to Him.
He is not merely a better version of the priests who came before Him.
He is the eternal High Priest who gave His own life for sinners.
The One who was rejected.
The One who was crucified.
The One who rose again.
The One who still intercedes for His people.
And the One who welcomes those who come to the Father through Him.
Maybe your story is full of chapters you wish you could erase.
Maybe there are choices you would undo if time could be turned backward.
Maybe you know what it feels like to lose something precious because of your own actions.
Or perhaps you have remained outwardly faithful while privately struggling with fear, temptation, disappointment, and spiritual exhaustion.
Hear this clearly.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem a life surrendered to Him today.
He does not promise to restore every lost position, reverse every consequence, or give back everything sin has taken.
He promises something infinitely greater to those who trust Him.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A living hope.
Eternal life.
And a future secured not by our flawless performance, but by His finished work.
That is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not that scandals are harmless.
It is that grace is real.
Not that sin has no consequences.
But that sin does not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Not that everyone automatically receives restoration regardless of repentance.
But that no repentant sinner needs to believe Christ is unable to save.
And if this story has uncovered something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to respond honestly.
Not for appearances.
Not to impress other believers.
But because sometimes admitting that we need prayer is the first courageous step toward seeking help.
Your story may encourage someone who believes their failure has placed them beyond hope.
Someone who once served passionately and now feels exhausted.
Someone who made a devastating mistake and no longer believes they can come back to God.
Because spiritual growth is not sustained by one emotional moment.
We need to keep returning to God's Word.
We need sound teaching.
We need Christian community.
We need correction when we drift and encouragement when we grow weary.
And above everything, we need Jesus.
This is also why we are committed to building and expanding the Gospel Warrior ministry.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who are hungry for biblical understanding, encouragement, healing, and spiritual maturity.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because financial support is a requirement for salvation or a replacement for faithful giving to your local church.
Grace cannot be bought. The Gospel is not for sale.
But Christian ministry does require people who willingly give their time, abilities, prayers, and resources.
Scripture teaches that supporting Gospel work can be a meaningful act of generosity and partnership (Philippians 4:15–18; 2 Corinthians 9:7).
Those items are simply expressions of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and they are not the reason anyone should give.
The deeper invitation is to become a consistent partner in a ministry devoted to making Christ known.
There is no shame in giving nothing financially.
The Lord sees the heart.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the kind of partnership we desire.
Willing.
Joyful.
Grounded in truth.
Centered on Jesus Christ.
And committed to serving people rather than pressuring them.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to direct hearts toward the Savior.
Abiathar's story reminds us that even those with extraordinary spiritual histories need humility and obedience.
Solomon's decision reminds us that actions have consequences.
The prophecy concerning Eli reminds us that God's Word stands.
But Jesus Christ reminds us that our deepest hope has never rested in an earthly priest, a royal appointment, or a flawless human record.
Our hope rests in the crucified and risen Savior.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, ask yourself something.
Am I following Jesus today, or am I living on the memory of when I used to follow Him closely?
Am I listening to His Word, or have I become skilled at defending what I already want?
Am I hiding behind my Christian reputation, or am I allowing the Lord to search my heart?
And if the answers are painful, do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
Abiathar lost his priestly office.
But the eternal High Priest still receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
The door to God's mercy is not opened by our titles, achievements, or spiritual résumés.
It is opened through Jesus Christ.
And that is where the story must leave us.
Not staring endlessly at the ruins of a fallen priest's position.
But looking to the Savior whose priesthood will never end.
Your greatest tragedy would not be losing the position you once held—it would be clinging to the appearance of faith while refusing the Savior who is calling you home.
